I wrote software for a local police department to support their bodycam implementation. They wanted no monthly fees, no vendor lock-in, and to save video for 180 days at a minimum.

I got them an 8 bay drobo with 3TB drives, bodycams which are USB mass storage devices when plugged in, and built a downloading station with a 16 port hub and a linux machine. The linux machine runs a script to MD5 and move the files to temp storage on the drobo when a camera is plugged in. Another script runs on a server which stores the files by date and MD5s them again after they are in final storage. After 191 days (strange IN law mentioned in the article) ffmpeg's AVCONV is run on the videos, compressing them to ~15% of original size. At 90% storage fill, videos are deleted by date until back down to > 90% disk utilization.

Upfront cost was around $2000 plus $300 for each camera. The major bodycam companies refuse to deal in upfront costs- they all charge exorbitant monthly fees- one I saw recently was $75 per camera per month.

If there was a commercial local-storage option on the market which allowed the customer to own their own equipment, bodycams would be a no-brainer, an easily justified cost. But since the only real options out now charge monthly, the justification isn't as simple.

I'd really love to partner with a more skilled programmer and make a commercial solution. We'd be rich.

EDIT: TL;DR: when companies are charging $75/mo/cop for camera and storage, that IS a significant budgetary hit. If there were a way for more departments to own their storage and not pay monthly, fees would be reasonable and affordable.

George Wythe (1726-1806) was Thomas Jefferson's legal mentor. Wythe was educated by his mother, passing the bar in York County in 1748. He rose in prominence and was elected a member of the House of Burgesses and to the office of attorney general.

William Small introduced Jefferson to Wythe when Jefferson was a student at the College of William and Mary. Small, Wythe, Governor Fauquier, and Jefferson shared many Palace dinners where Jefferson received an "unofficial" political and cultural education. Jefferson would study law under Wythe from 1762 until 1767.

In 1775, Wythe joined Richard Henry Lee, Jefferson, Benjamin Harrison, Thomas Nelson Jr., Francis Lightfoot Lee, and Carter Braxton at the Continental Congress. Wythe became one of the signers of the Declaration of Independence. After returning to Virginia, Wythe played a role in creating the state's new constitution and served with Jefferson on the committee that revised Virginia's laws. Wythe also sat on the committee to design Virginia's seal.

In 1779, Wythe assumed a professorship of law and policy at the College of William and Mary and remained there until 1789. He served as a judge on the High Court of Chancery and was elected as a Virginia delegate to the Constitutional Convention, but resigned due to his wife's illness. He died in 1806, apparently poisoned by his grandnephew, George Sweeney.
